beats.narration: Begin by framing Program Overview and Status as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. When registered for co-op, students are considered by RIT to have full-time status. Consider this worked case: A student enrolled in CSCI-499 for the fall semester is counted as a full-time undergraduate for financial aid and housing purposes. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Program Overview and Status
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a simple badge graphic labeled 'Full-Time Status' next to a calendar showing a 14-week span.

beats.narration: Now define Time Commitment Requirements precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. In order to register for co-op for either fall or spring semester, we expect that students will work a minimum of 14 weeks and work a minimum of 35 hours per week. Consider this worked case: A student planning a spring co-op must schedule at least 490 hours of work spread across the semester. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Time Commitment Requirements
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a bar chart comparing a 14-week minimum schedule against a 12-week schedule, highlighting the 35-hour weekly threshold.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Prerequisite Coursework operates in a concrete sequence. Students must complete a student co-op work report for each term for which they are registered; students are also evaluated each term by their supervisor. Consider this worked case: A student who has not taken CSCI-099 must enroll in it first to become eligible for the co-op program. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Prerequisite Coursework
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a linear prerequisite flowchart: 'CSCI-099' -> 'Eligible for CSCI-499 Co-op'.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Student Work Report Requirement and make the decision criteria explicit. A satisfactory grade is given for co-op when both a completed student co-op work report and a completed, corresponding supervisor evaluation are received and when both documents are generally consistent. Consider this worked case: A student working on a software development project must submit a written report detailing their tasks, challenges, and outcomes. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Student Work Report Requirement
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a document template with sections for 'Project Description', 'Technical Implementation', and 'Learning Outcomes'.

beats.narration: Apply Supervisor Evaluation Requirement to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Students perform professional work related to Computer Science. Consider this worked case: A supervisor reviews the student's code commits and deliverables to provide a formal performance evaluation. 'Supervisor Evaluation' with a checkmark indicating consistency. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Supervisor Evaluation Requirement
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a two-column comparison: 'Student Report' vs. 'Supervisor Evaluation' with a checkmark indicating consistency.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Grading Consistency Standard, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Consider this worked case: If the student report describes a database migration but the supervisor evaluation focuses solely on UI testing, the grade is not satisfactory. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Grading Consistency Standard
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Use a Venn diagram showing the overlap between 'Student Report Content' and 'Supervisor Evaluation Content' as the grading zone.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Ethical Computing Principles with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. Consider this worked case: A co-op student developing an AI model must audit training data for bias and document limitations to prevent harmful outcomes. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Ethical Computing Principles
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a checklist graphic with icons for 'Avoid Harm', 'Honesty', 'High Quality', and 'Respect Privacy'.

beats.narration: Use Responsible Research Communication to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. Consider this worked case: A student's co-op report must include a literature review section that cites existing algorithms before presenting new results. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Responsible Research Communication
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-by-side comparison of a 'Misleading Claim' (highlighted in red) versus a 'Responsible Claim' (highlighted in green) with citations.

beats.narration: Connect Research Integrity and Transparency to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Consider this worked case: A co-op project report must include a dedicated section listing data collection constraints and potential biases in the experimental setup. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Research Integrity and Transparency
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a template slide with a 'Limitations & Threats' box and a 'Conflicts Disclosure' field to be filled by students.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Consider this worked case: Before final submission, a student checks that their 14-week schedule is logged, their report matches the supervisor's evaluation, and all ethical guidelines are met. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a final checklist graphic with four checkboxes: '14-Week/35-Hr Commitment', 'Report-Evaluation Consistency', 'Ethical Compliance', 'Research Transparency'.

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.
sources.title: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

sources.author: Association for Computing Machinery
sources.excerpt: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.
